name: Tomas Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm operations lead on Ridgeway Estate, which an investment fund bought six years ago. It's about five hundred hectares of wheat and beans, a sow unit with four hundred sows, and a small biogas plant that eats the slurry. I start at seven with the pig team's report on my phone, then I'm out checking crops with a drone, sorting the feed ratios, and in meetings with the land agent who answers to people in an office I've never seen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the puzzles: getting the feed right so the pigs grow faster on less, or reading a drone map and catching blackgrass before it spreads. What wears me out is the pay and the people above. I'm paid less than the farm's spending on software some years, and after my little cut-flower business went under two years ago, we've had almost nothing saved. Ingrid, my partner, works part time as a vet nurse, and with two kids and the mortgage it's tight every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I was a bit disappointed, to be honest. I use AI every day to check feed ratios and to read the drone maps, and it's already handy. I'd post that the real gains in farming were always going to come from robots and soil, not from chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's safe and my pay stays poor. I'd go on doing clever things for a fund that doesn't notice. That's not a disaster, it's just slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I've got and keep pushing the land agent for a bonus tied to the savings I make. I'd probably go to the open day at the agricultural college to look at the small robots anyway, because I can't help myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit bored. A plateau is fine, but it's not the future anyone promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the cut-flower business.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I grew dahlias and sweet peas on a rented field and sold them to florists. A wet summer and a supplier going bust finished it, and we lost about eight thousand. It taught me to love risk a bit more carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who gets the savings you make on the estate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fund. I saved them forty thousand on feed last year and got a thank-you email. That's what I'd change if I could change one thing.

S0.say: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, because I use AI every day for feed ratios and drone maps and it already helps. The real gains in farming were always going to be robots and soil, not chatbots.
S0.think: My job's safe and my pay stays poor. I'd keep doing clever things for a fund that doesn't notice, which isn't a disaster, just slow.
S0.do: Keeps using his current AI tools and presses the land agent for a bonus tied to the feed savings he makes. Visits the agricultural college open day to look at small robots out of curiosity.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly bored, since a plateau is safe but not the future he hoped for.
S0.quote: I saved them forty thousand on feed last year and got a thank-you email.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas is the rare farmer who finds the hype picture disappointing. His thin savings come from a failed cut-flower business, which he talks about without shame. The real grievance is who keeps the value he creates, and that theme came up straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good, if workers share in it. I'd be the one at the farming discussion group telling people to try things. Online I'd be arguing that the fund should share savings with staff, and that the government should help small farms buy kit too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this suits me. I'm the person on the estate who already knows how the systems work. If they bring in a robot feeder or a camera that spots lame sows, someone has to set it up, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to run the first trial on the estate, probably a robot weeder in the beans in year one. I'd do the online course on farm robotics in the evenings, which costs a few hundred. And I'd ask the land agent in writing for a pay rise tied to running the new systems, because if not now, never.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. There's a little knot about the pig lads, but mostly I'd be keen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the knot about the pig lads?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Darren and Kasia do the feeding and the washing down. If a robot does the feeding, the fund will want one of them gone. I'd fight to move them onto the robots with me, but I don't make that call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the course with nothing saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the estate to pay, and if they said no I'd put it on the card and cut the takeaway on Fridays. Ingrid would roll her eyes, but she'd agree.

S1.say: This is good if workers share in it. I'd be telling people at the discussion group to try things, and arguing online that funds should share the savings with staff.
S1.think: This suits me, because I'm the one on the estate who already knows how the systems work. If a robot feeder or a lameness camera arrives, someone has to set it up, and that's me.
S1.do: Volunteers to run the estate's first robot weeder trial in the beans in the first year and takes an evening course on farm robotics. Asks in writing for a pay rise tied to running the new systems and cuts small treats to pay for the course if needed.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with a small knot of worry about the pig team.
S1.quote: If a robot does the feeding, the fund will want one of them gone.
S1.fieldNote: This is the scenario where he lights up. He's honest that it suits him and equally honest that it threatens two workmates, and he knows he doesn't make that decision. He'd fund his own retraining on a credit card, which shows both his appetite for risk and how thin his cushion is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast and the people who own the land and the robots will take everything unless the government steps in. I'd be calling for a tax on robots and a basic income while it settles. I'd say it loudly, even though I love the tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd lose my job too. Right now I'm useful because I understand the systems better than anyone. With full AGI, the systems understand themselves. The fund could run Ridgeway from a laptop in another country.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month, I'd sit down with Ingrid and cut everything except the mortgage, food and the kids' clubs. I'd try to get hired by one of the robot companies as a field technician, because there'll be a short window where they need people who know farms. I'd also join the farmworkers' union, which I've never bothered with, because this is the moment for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the one who's excited, and this is the first time I'd feel the floor go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Elsa, your daughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's fourteen and she follows all this stuff more than I do. I'd tell her the truth, that her dad's job will probably go but he'll find something. I'd make sure she saw me trying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you love risk. Does that help here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some. I'd jump at a new job faster than most. But risk is fine when you've got eight thousand to lose, and right now I don't.

S2.say: This is going too fast, and the people who own the land and robots will take everything unless the government steps in. We'd need a robot tax and a basic income while it settles.
S2.think: I'd lose my job too. Right now I'm useful because I understand the systems best, but with full AGI the systems understand themselves and the fund could run the estate from a laptop abroad.
S2.do: Cuts household spending to mortgage, food and the children's clubs in the first month. Applies to robot companies as a farm field technician while the window is open, and joins the farmworkers' union for the first time.
S2.feel: Alarmed; for the first time the usual excitement gives way to feeling the floor go.
S2.quote: With full AGI, the systems understand themselves. The fund could run Ridgeway from a laptop in another country.
S2.fieldNote: The adaptive mindset hits its limit here: his edge is knowing the systems, and fast AGI makes that edge worthless. He would still move quickly, toward a technician job, but his lack of savings makes risk feel different. Joining a union for the first time was a telling shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, and farm workers should be first in line for retraining money, not last. I'd be in the union by then, pushing for a deal where the estate keeps people on to run and repair the kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be all right for most of the five years and then hit a wall. I'd be the person who installed the systems that replaced me, which is a strange thought. I'd be forty-eight and need a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd get certified on farm robot repair and setup, probably a twelve-week course. I'd start a small side business doing drone crop scouting for neighbouring farms at weekends, to build some savings and contacts. By year three I'd want to be working for a robot dealer or myself, not the fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with my sleeves rolled up. I'd feel like I was racing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. With two years I'm scrambling for a job. With five, I can build a business and some savings first, and maybe leave on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about the kids' future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas is eight, so by 2031 he's thirteen and it's all a blur. Elsa would be choosing what to study. I'd tell her to pick something with people in it, like nursing or teaching, because I don't know what else is safe.

S3.say: Five years is short but workable, and farmworkers should be first in line for retraining money. The estate should keep people on to run and repair the kit.
S3.think: I'd be fine for most of the five years and then hit a wall. I'd be the one who installed the systems that replaced me, at 48 and needing a new trade.
S3.do: Takes a twelve-week certification in farm robot repair and setup in the first year and starts weekend drone scouting for neighbouring farms to build savings. Aims to be working for a robot dealer or himself by the third year, and steers his daughter toward work with people.
S3.feel: Anxious but with his sleeves rolled up, like racing against it.
S3.quote: I'd be the person who installed the systems that replaced me, which is a strange thought.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets his adaptability work: he plans a certification, a side business and an exit on his own terms. He's aware of the irony of installing his own replacement. His advice to his daughter, to pick work with people in it, was quick and uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this fairly, and I'd be pushing for robots on farms to be shared or co-owned, not just bought up by funds. I'd say farmworkers should get a slice of every saving a robot makes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well out of this. By 2036 I'd have ten years of experience with farm robots, and someone will still need to plan, check and fix. The pay worry doesn't go away, but I'd have time to build up savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the robotics course this year anyway, then build up the scouting business slowly while still at Ridgeway. Over the decade I'd want to set up a small co-op with three or four other farm techs, so we own the kit and rent it to farms. I'd also want Ingrid's job to be safe, so she might move toward animal physiotherapy, which she's been talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a hopeful way. There's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If everything goes to robots, what's left for a person like you to do in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm not sure. Maybe deciding what to grow and why, and making sure it's done right by the animals and the land. But I'd be lying if I said I knew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who'll own it all, if they don't share. Not the robots, they don't choose anything. And the government, if it watches and does nothing for ten years.

S4.say: Ten years is a real chance to do this fairly. Farm robots should be shared or co-owned rather than bought up by funds, and farmworkers should get a slice of every saving.
S4.think: I think I'd do well out of this, with ten years of robot experience by the time it lands. The pay worry doesn't go away, but I'd have time to build savings.
S4.do: Starts the robotics course this year and slowly grows the drone scouting business while staying at the estate. Works over the decade toward a small technicians' cooperative that owns kit and rents it to farms, and supports his partner moving into animal physiotherapy.
S4.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, with room to breathe.
S4.quote: Not the robots, they don't choose anything.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, he sees himself as a winner, though he's honest that he doesn't know what humans will do once AGI arrives. His plan to co-own robots with other technicians joins his progressive politics with his love of the kit. He blames owners and inaction, not technology.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would take away the one thing I'm good at before I'd had time to turn it into something. What would help is a fund for retraining that farmworkers can actually use, and rules so the savings from robots get shared with the people who worked the land.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd still want to farm. I would. I'd want to farm with the robots, not be replaced by them. There's a difference, and it's mostly about who owns them.

headlineQuote: I'd want to farm with the robots, not be replaced by them. There's a difference, and it's mostly about who owns them.
portrait: Tomas Larsen is a 43-year-old operations lead on a fund-owned pig and arable estate who uses AI every day and loves a technical puzzle, but has almost no savings after a cut-flower business failed. He's slightly bored by the hype picture and excited by steady change, where he'd run the first robot trials. A two-year AGI arrival frightens him because it would make his technical edge worthless before he'd saved anything. With five or ten years he plans retraining, a side business and a technicians' cooperative, and his anger is aimed at owners who don't share, not the machines.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it would take away the skill he's best at before he could turn it into something new.
whatWouldHelp: A retraining fund farmworkers can actually use, and rules so the savings from robots are shared with the people who work the land.
